analysis.one_liner: Bars credit bureaus from selling mortgage shoppers' information to other lenders as leads.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop credit bureaus from selling mortgage applicants' data to other lenders was introduced with bipartisan support but died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When you apply for a mortgage, the credit bureaus see your inquiry and sell your name as a "trigger lead" to other mortgage lenders, who then call you — sometimes many times a day — while you shop for a loan. This bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop that: credit bureaus could no longer sell a credit report to anyone you didn't initiate contact with, when the only reason they found you was your mortgage inquiry [S2][S3]. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People shopping for a home mortgage, who currently get cold-called by competing lenders — often several a day — as soon as their credit is pulled. The bill also protects anyone who doesn't want their loan shopping quietly broadcast to strangers. Homeowners facing foreclosure or loan modification would be especially protected, since scammers target those inquiries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People applying for a home mortgage

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits credit reporting agencies from selling a credit report to a lender the consumer never contacted, when the trigger is a mortgage credit inquiry [S2][S3].
Amends Section 604(c) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the same provision lenders use today to buy trigger leads, so the ban applies nationwide to all bureaus [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three big credit bureaus, which earn fees selling trigger leads, and mortgage lenders and lead brokers who rely on those purchased lists to find customers. Some smaller lenders argue the practice helps them compete against the biggest banks, and could see fewer inbound customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and lead-buying mortgage lenders

drawbacks.text: Critics of banning trigger leads argue the calls create price competition: smaller lenders use leads to offer borrowers rates that might beat their bank's quote, so a ban could mean fewer competing offers [S3] and, in the industry's view, less competition.
The ban is absolute — it blocks all non-initiated mortgage-related furnishing, with no consumer opt-in option, so borrowers who might welcome competing offers lose the chance to receive them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is privacy and peace of mind for millions of mortgage shoppers — no more daily cold calls triggered by your own credit check. The main cost falls on the bureaus and lenders who monetize the data, plus some loss of extra competing offers for borrowers who liked getting them. A narrower opt-in design might have balanced those interests better, but the core consumer harm the bill targets is real and one-sided: the consumer never asked to be sold.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on April 17, 2023, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) introduced the Trigger Leads Abatement Act on April 17, 2023 [S1][S5].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record through the end of the 118th Congress [S5].
Six members cosponsored the bill: five House Democrats and one House Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus keep the right to sell mortgage shoppers' data as trigger leads, and the lead-buying lenders keep the pipeline. Mortgage shoppers keep getting the calls.

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act and ban trigger leads for mortgage loans [S1][S3].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 17, 2023 and took no further recorded action — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — five Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — but neither party brought it to the floor; there were no recorded votes or recorded opposition in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Bureaus sell trigger leads — consumers' mortgage inquiries — to competing lenders for a fee, without the consumer asking. The bill would end that revenue stream, which is why consumer groups back trigger-lead bans and the bureaus oppose them. Sources: the bill directly prohibits the practice [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and lead brokers that buy trigger leads
industries.note: These lenders buy lists of mortgage shoppers and cold-call them for business. Some borrowers do get a better rate from an unsolicited call, but the calls are unwanted by most shoppers and can drown out the lender the consumer actually chose [S2].
